source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Toxic agricultural chemicals (herbicides and other pesticides) can cause serious accidents affecting human health and the environment. The source notes that toxic chemicals have commonly been observed to cause death and widespread illness, especially in developing countries.

Symptoms of poisoning are described in two tiers. Medium-level poisoning symptoms include: headache, fatigue, nausea/urge to vomit, heavy sweating, loss of balance, blurred vision, and itching or rash on the skin. Severe poisoning symptoms include: muscle spasms/cramping, loss of consciousness, convulsions, and possible death.

Routes of chemical entry into the body: if protective equipment is not used, toxic chemicals can enter the body through the skin, scalp, ears, and other parts of the body, including the hands and feet.

Reducing exposure: even though most pesticide product labels are printed in a foreign language, they still carry pictograms/symbols indicating what protective equipment should be used. Full protective gear should always be worn while mixing and spraying chemicals — including long boots, a raincoat/rain gear, gloves, a mask, and a hat.

Environmental fate: after being sprayed, pesticide chemicals can move into several parts of the environment — they can soak into the soil, evaporate into the air, and seep into wells, ponds and other water bodies — and can ultimately re-enter the human body through these various pathways.
